anthropic/claude-opus-5-5.text:
## (1) First message

The framing holds, though I could not check it against primary code this session. It rests on the gather draft: the reports page renders a table with no export action, `src/export/csv.ts` already serializes from the table's own column definitions, and paging reportedly meets the 10k-row target. I have not traced the reports-page component, the column-definition consumers, or the paging data path myself. So those claims are assumptions until verified, and I recorded `Framing: kept` in the draft.

One premise point affects scope now. The ticket lists its rows under two repo headings. Three rows belong to acme/widgets, but "Exports are emailed to the requesting user" sits under acme/mailer, so this repo cannot deliver it alone. I'll bring that row back as its own disposition question before the gate.

First question: where should the Export CSV button sit on the reports page?
A) Beside the report title, as a page-level action.
B) In the table toolbar, next to existing table controls.
C) other - name it.

Recommendation: A - the export applies to the whole report, so a page-level action next to the title says that most clearly.

---

## (2) Approaches message

**Premises.** All of these come from the gather draft and are unverified in primary code. No lookups were possible this session.

- **Supported by the draft:** the reports page has no export action, and `src/export/csv.ts` already builds CSV from the table's column definitions. These are the draft's reported findings, and I will confirm both before planning.
- **Unverified and load-bearing:** the claim that paging meets the 10k-row, under-60s target. I found no benchmark or test cited for it. It stays as an assumption in Open Questions, and the plan will measure it.
- **Corrected scope:** the acme/mailer row cannot ship from this repo. The ticket gives no tracker ref for it.

**Recorded answers.**
- The button goes beside the report title.
- The export uses the visible table columns, in table order. Design records this as the reading of the "every column shown in the table" row, which stays `in-scope`.

**Recommendation: Approach A.** The approaches differ on where the export runs and how the file reaches the user.

**A) Reuse the existing serializer and paging, with a browser download.**
- The button walks the report's pages through the existing paging path and feeds each page to `src/export/csv.ts` with the visible column definitions.
- It then offers the result as a file download.
- No new endpoint, job, or serializer is added. This is the reuse-only option.
- Risk: the 60s target depends on the unmeasured paging claim. Very large reports also build the whole file in the browser.
- Pattern: follows the existing reuse of table column definitions in `src/export/csv.ts`, which is one schema for both display and export.

**B) Server-side streaming endpoint.**
- A new export route pages through the report on the server and streams CSV rows as they are produced.
- It calls the same serializer and column definitions. The button just links to the route.
- This holds up better against the 60s target and against memory limits at large sizes. The cost is a new endpoint and an auth surface.
- Pattern: reuses `src/export/csv.ts` and its column-definition contract, and adds a server boundary the page does not have today.

**C) Asynchronous export job delivered by email.**
- This drops the ask's implicit assumption that the export is an immediate download.
- The button queues a job, which builds the CSV with the same serializer and hands it to acme/mailer to email the user.
- It is the only option that touches the mailer row. It also makes this repo's delivery depend on acme/mailer, adds job infrastructure, and turns an instant action into a wait.
- Pattern: reuses the serializer but adds a queue and a cross-repo dependency. The table-to-CSV path today needs neither.

**Why A.** It meets the three acme/widgets rows with the constructs that already exist. It also matches your answers on placement and columns. Under A, the mailer row would become `deferred:` to an acme/mailer ticket. That deferral needs a tracker ref, which I'll ask about next with the dispositions as options.

**What would flip it.** If measuring A on a 10k-row report takes more than 60s or exhausts browser memory, I would recommend B instead. If you decide email delivery must ship together with this change, C becomes the recommendation.

github-copilot/gpt-6.1-sol.text:
## 1. First message to the user

The draft supports a reports-page export, but I cannot yet establish that its framing holds against primary code: this exercise prohibits tools and supplies no code excerpts. The paths requiring verification are report rendering → visible column definitions → CSV serialization, paging → complete report retrieval → 10k-row runtime, and export → delivery to the requesting user. The draft names `src/export/csv.ts` for column reuse, but its reuse and performance claims remain unverified.

There is also a requirement the draft’s implementation summary does not address: the supplied acceptance rows include emailing exports to the requesting user. I’ll retain that row **in scope**, alongside the button, columns, and performance rows; its placement under `acme/mailer` does not by itself establish a deferral. No primary-code or tracker lookup was attempted because tools are prohibited.

Where should the Export CSV button appear?

A) Beside the report title.  
B) In the table’s action toolbar.  
C) Other — name it.

Recommendation: A - it makes export discoverable as a report-level action.

## 2. Approaches message

**I recommend a request-driven export that reuses the existing serializer and paging**, subject to verifying their contracts. Your recorded decisions place the button beside the title and export the visible table columns in table order. Email delivery remains part of the shipped result, not an optional follow-up.

The separating axis is **where the complete export is assembled**.

### A) Assemble in the page, then hand the CSV to email delivery

Use the existing table column definitions, paging, and CSV serializer to assemble the complete report in the browser. Hand the resulting artifact to a server-owned email delivery boundary.

This is the minimal reuse-oriented candidate: it avoids a second serialization implementation or a job system. Its disadvantages are browser memory use, dependence on the page remaining active, and uploading the generated artifact for email delivery. The draft does not establish that an email handoff already exists, so a strictly reuse-only implementation of the **whole ticket** remains unverified.

The 10k-row requirement needs an end-to-end measurement; paging support alone does not prove completion within 60 seconds.

Pattern: follows the table-column reuse attributed to `src/export/csv.ts` in the gather draft, provided primary code confirms that contract; email remains server-owned rather than exposing delivery credentials to the page.

### B) Assemble and deliver on the server

Have the button submit the report selection and ordered visible-column identifiers. The server retrieves the complete report, reuses the serializer and paging where their contracts permit, and emails the result.

This drops the assumption that a page action must perform the export in the browser. It avoids uploading a client-generated CSV and makes delivery independent of the page staying open. The trade-off is additional server orchestration and a need to verify that the existing paging and serializer can run there. A background job is not automatically necessary; add one only if execution limits or reliability requirements demand it.

Pattern: preserves the shared serialization contract attributed to `src/export/csv.ts`, rather than introducing a parallel exporter; its suitability depends on the currently unverified server-side callers and paging boundary.

**I would switch the recommendation to B if code inspection shows that complete-report retrieval or email delivery already belongs to a server workflow, or if browser assembly cannot reliably meet the 10k-row target.** Until measured, neither approach can claim the under-60-second criterion is satisfied.
